say.text: Two infants, both with TOF on echo. Baby A is a cyanotic neonate.
Baby B, not diagnosed before birth, is asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur.
What most plausibly separates B from A?

choices.label: B's RVOT resistance is lower than his systemic resistance
B's echo must be wrong: every TOF is blue from birth
B's pulmonary vascular resistance is lower than A's
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think of cyanosis as a balance between two resistances: the one across the RVOT and the one in the body's circulation. In a pink baby, which of the two is lower?
Yes. When resistance across the RVOT is less than systemic vascular resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
Moderate obstruction with only a loud murmur is the 'pink Tet'.
Tempting, because TOF is the most common cyanotic heart disease and usually presents as a cyanotic neonate.
But 'usually' is not 'always': infants with moderate obstruction can be asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur, the 'pink Tets'.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the contrast: A and B share the diagnosis and differ in how much obstruction there is.

say.text: It is tempting to look at the lungs, since cyanosis means too little blood reaching them. But the balance that decides it sits between the RVOT and the body.
If RVOT resistance is below systemic vascular resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note which two resistances are being compared: RVOT versus systemic, not pulmonary.

say.text: A classmate says: 'TOF is cyanotic heart disease, so every TOF baby is blue at birth.'
Which reply fits the source best?

choices.label: Most present as a cyanotic neonate, but a pink Tet is possible
Agreed: acyanotic TOF does not exist
Pink Tets have a lower pulmonary resistance than blue ones

say.text: Right. TOF most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate, yet moderate obstruction can give a pink Tet.
Both babies share one diagnosis and sit at different points on the RVOT-versus-systemic balance.
It sounds neat because the label is 'cyanotic' and the usual presentation matches it.
But infants with moderate obstruction may be asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur. Those are pink Tets.
This feels logical because cyanosis is about the lungs. The rule in the source compares two other resistances.
The child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic when RVOT resistance is below systemic vascular resistance.
Now the murmur. At baseline, the greater the obstruction, the more prominent the murmur.
Hold that rule and look at the same baby on a bad day.
A 4-month-old with TOF is crying, deeply cyanosed and breathing fast. Agitation is a known trigger of a tet spell.
Compared with a calm clinic visit, the murmur is now probably:

choices.label: Louder, as the obstruction has worsened
Unchanged, as the anatomy is the same
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask one question: with the baby in this state, how much blood is actually crossing the RVOT right now?
Yes. During a tet spell there is a decrease in the intensity of the murmur.
The reason: with significant obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta and bypasses the pulmonary bed, so less crosses the RVOT.
Tempting, because the baseline rule says more obstruction, more prominent murmur.
But a spell is not the baseline: the intensity of the murmur decreases, as blood shunts toward the aorta instead of crossing the RVOT.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: the baseline rule and the spell rule point in opposite directions, and the spell rule wins in a spell.

say.text: Tempting, since the anatomy has not changed. What changes in a spell is how much blood goes through it.
The murmur decreases in intensity during a tet spell.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember the murmur follows flow across the RVOT, not just the anatomy.

say.text: A mother says: 'Last week you heard a loud murmur, now it is faint, so he must be better.'
The child is blue and distressed. Best reading?

choices.label: A spell: the murmur falls because less blood crosses the RVOT

say.text: Yes. A fall in murmur intensity fits a spell, in which most blood bypasses the pulmonary bed.
Reasonable if you read loudness as severity, as the baseline rule does.
But a spell reduces the murmur's intensity, and the child is distressed, which points away from improvement.
Heart failure is a familiar cause of a distressed, breathless baby, so it draws the eye.
Here the TOF-specific explanation is a spell: agitation is a trigger, and the murmur gets softer.
The murmur is harsh systolic ejection, best heard at the left mid to upper sternal border, with posterior radiation.
Next the second sound. Many pulmonary lesions bring a loud P2 to mind. Test that against TOF.
Most blood bypasses the pulmonary bed in significant obstruction.
What is the pulmonic component of S2 in TOF?

choices.label: Loud, as in other pulmonary lesions
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Picture the pulmonary valve in a baby where little blood reaches it. Would you expect a crisp closing sound?
Yes. The pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible in TOF.
A loud P2 is tempting because the word 'pulmonary' suggests a high-pressure lung circuit.
In TOF the pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one matters: ask how much blood reaches the pulmonary valve, and the answer is inaudible.

say.text: Splitting is a common S2 theme, so it attracts a pick.
The source says the pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible, so there is nothing to split.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair TOF with one phrase: harsh ejection murmur, inaudible P2.

say.text: Last contrast, with no hint. Three findings fit TOF and one does not.
Which does NOT fit?

choices.label: A loud pulmonic component of S2
A murmur that softens during a spell
A pink infant with a loud murmur and TOF on echo
An inaudible pulmonic component of S2

say.text: Right. The pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible, so a loud one does not fit.
The other three do fit: a softer murmur in a spell, a pink Tet, and an inaudible P2.
It looks odd at first, as more obstruction normally means a more prominent murmur.
But it does fit: in a spell the murmur intensity decreases.
